name: Authoritarian capitalism
summary: Authoritarian capitalism is a regime type in which a market economy with mostly market-set prices and private and state firms runs under an authoritarian state: power is concentrated in a small elite, there is no independent legislature or judiciary, and speech, press, opposition and civil society are tightly controlled. The sources describe it as nationalist, integrated into the global economy, and hostile to liberal claims of universal values; Lee Kuan Yew's Singapore is its model case. The authoritarian neoliberalism strand (Edozie after Bruff) is the critical reading of the same pairing of market discipline with state power.
scope: A regime model in which a market economy with private property and market prices runs under an authoritarian state that restricts dissent and has no independent legislature or courts, as the defining scholarship and commentary describe it: Friedberg's 'nationalist authoritarian capitalism' of China and Russia (s1), Drezner on China's leaders' bid to loosen the economy while tightening politics (s2), Cassidy's account of Lee Kuan Yew's Singapore as its model (s3), John Lee's contrast of Chinese and Russian authoritarian capitalism with Western capitalism (s4), and Scheiring's account of Orbán's Hungary (s5). Its one named thinker is Lee Kuan Yew. The redirect 'authoritarian neoliberalism' is taken in Edozie's sense (s6, after Bruff): the neoliberal state insulated from democratic pressure, typified in Asia by the China model. Excluded: Deng Xiaoping's own Marxist-Leninist texts (his thought has its own profile, Deng Xiaoping Theory), Pinochetism, Putinism and other regime-specific ideologies, and Western liberal democracies as such. It is a regime type with commentators and a few defenders rather than a codified doctrine, so positions come from what those sources say the model holds.

sources.title: Authoritarian capitalism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Definition, examples, defenders and critics, themes of markets, state firms, protectionism and regime stability.

sources.title: Uphold the Four Cardinal Principles (1979)
sources.author: Deng Xiaoping
sources.usedFor: A Marxist-Leninist speech by the architect of China's reforms: Party leadership, socialist rather than bourgeois democracy, condemnation of disruptive protest; also its affirmation of class struggle and proletarian dictatorship. It does not discuss markets.

sources.title: Lee Kuan Yew quotations
sources.author: Lee Kuan Yew (speeches and interviews, compiled on Wikiquote)
sources.usedFor: Lee's statements on democracy and development, the press, family, meritocracy, one-party rule and self-reliance.

sources.title: Asian values
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Primacy of group over individual, Bangkok Declaration, sovereignty and the cultural-relativist argument.

sources.title: State capitalism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: State-owned enterprises, state direction of investment, retained wage labour and profit.

sources.title: Excerpts from talks given in Wuchang, Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Shanghai (1992)
sources.author: Deng Xiaoping
sources.usedFor: Deng's reform-era case that a market economy is not capitalism, growth of productive forces as the criterion, foreign-funded firms, praise of Singapore's strict order, and continued Marxist commitments.

sources.title: The Authoritarian Challenge: China, Russia and the Threat to the Liberal International Order
sources.author: Aaron L. Friedberg (Sasakawa Peace Foundation, 2017)
sources.usedFor: Scholarly account of 'nationalist authoritarian capitalism' in China and Russia: concentrated power without independent legislatures or judiciaries, state capitalism with market prices, global integration, nationalism and patriotic education, surveillance, NGO and internet control, rejection of universal values.

sources.title: Can Authoritarian Capitalism Outlive Lee Kuan Yew?
sources.author: John Cassidy, The New Yorker (2015)
sources.usedFor: Lee Kuan Yew's Singapore as the model of authoritarian capitalism and its influence on China.

sources.title: Western Vs. Authoritarian Capitalism
sources.author: John Lee, The Diplomat (2009)
sources.usedFor: The case for and against authoritarian capitalism as a rival to the Western model.

sources.title: Neoliberal democracy vs neoliberal authoritarianism: capitalism and democracy’s global contest in the twenty-first century (ch. 5 of Research Handbook on Democracy and Development)
sources.author: Rita Kiki Edozie, in Crawford and Abdulai (eds), Edward Elgar (2021)
sources.usedFor: Authoritarian neoliberalism after Bruff, typified in Asia by the China model.

notes: Authoritarian capitalism is a regime label described mostly by commentators, so only features the defining sources present as common to the model are answered; positions on policy detail, religion, family, territory and welfare are null. Themes searched: government, economy, liberty, world, culture, globalism, technology.
